title: Traditional slow start VS being thrown into action

posts.author: 3rr0r1n5ynt4x
posts.body:
When designing my current intro I was contemplating between 2 different possibilities:
1. Take the traditional slow start where you meet the hero, accompany him through a short patch of time and then something happens and the journey begins
2. Take the more action oriented approach where you get thrown right into the game and it's mechanics.
A good example for 2 would be Persona 5 where you get thrown in a near-endgame dungeon where you have to solve a short passage (without real danger of failing), meet many of the later characters etc.
I currently tend to chose the second approach. I see many advantages because I can show off some of the more "unique" mechanics of the game right away, show how combat looks and what possibilities you will have without going into too much detail, stir up some mystery like "how did we end up here?" etc.
However, I'm struggling because there is only one point in time where this actually makes sense and it has a much darker tone than most of the rest of the game, so people might get the wrong impression about what to expect in terms of tone.
What your opinion about those 2 different intro styles? Is there maybe another that you prefer to use?

posts.author: LordOfPotatos
posts.body:
the intro is a vertical slice of the whole thing. make clear what the thing is about and what the aesthetics are.
persona 5 is a good example, it shows off a lot of flashy style with little plot and puts you on a fight you can't lose if you're paying basic attention. truly the whole game in 5 minutes.
after that you can start establishing status quo and stuff.
though personally I'd use a different POV instead of in media res. showing an action scene from the middle of the plot at the start makes it giga obvious that you're just checking the action intro box.

posts.author: JohnDoeGames
posts.body:
I don't mind thrown into action, as long as a learning curve is offered. At least if this is required.
As you describe the intro scene of the approach: You have to fight your way trough easy to beat troops... That seems like a great approach for a turn-based RPG. Note that you can even add dialogue to the battles with troop events or before or after battle in the enemy events.
Story and action can go hand in hand pretty well in RPG maker.

posts.author: Robro33
posts.body:
I lean towards preferring 2. Starting with action is an easy way to hook a person into a setting, but imo the action itself is an effective way to show the players details about the world, the characters, and their goals before words alone could set in.
Spoiler:
first 10 minutes of xenoblade
like, Xenoblade 1 could have started with taking control of Shulk and telling you that the monado is the only thing that can effectively damage mechon, but starting with Dunban as the only person capable of damaging the mechon because he wields the mondado during a battle where only he and those immediately around him can be affected by it says way more about the nature of the battle for everyone else than just saying it.

posts.author: JohnDoeGames
posts.body:
If you're looking for more good examples where you jump into action: Final Fantasy X
What they did well, is they explained the moves during battle. If you script your first battles, you can not only add dialogue, also explain the battle system while you go.
For example you can have tell the player to use attack the first battle, during their first furn. And in the second battle, you disable attack for the first turn, and tell the player to guard. Then enable the attack in the second turn and tell the player to finish the enemy off. Then disable attack and guard for the first turn in the 3rd fight and tell the player to use an item.
You can do that in-character to build story as well. Have an in-game character tell the player: "Oh, a rat! Attack it now!", then have that in-game character say: "Careful, a jumping spider is charging an attack! You should use guard to avoid damage! NOW!" and in the third fight. "More rats? Here, take this smoke grenade. It will kill some, maybe even all of them!"
I don't know, it is just a simple example based on the basic RPG maker in-game functions I made up on the spot. You'd have to come up with something that fits your game, your characters and your battle system.
It is really simple to do with troop events, no plugins required at all. You start right into action and you can still have some story building, and explain the game as you go.
---
While writing this I just have many idea's on how a game in a wild action scene can start:
PC = Player Character
Spoiler:
Idea 1: Unexpected transformation
The player starts in battle with a young woman, and has only defensive skills enabled. The woman is shouting at him, she's scared and angry, causing a debuff on the player each turn. (This can be scripted, no real skills need to be made for this)
PC will ask that he did wrong before casting defensive spells/guard.
In a few turns it turns out PC had a blackout transformed. As a werewolf it attacked some sheep.
Then change the tint to "night", make a wolf howling sound and change your PC with a Wolf or Werewolf character. (This might require a plugin, although you can fade-out, then add the wolf, remove the human, fade in. Do the same thing in reverse to transform back. Make sure you add first, then remove. Otherwise your character might not be removed, if it is the only character in the party and you and up with 2 versions of your PC in the party at the same time... And thinking of it, this might only work if PC is the only character in the party.)
Spoiler:
Idea 2: End boss in scene one
You can even, if you want a super crazy action intro, have the player fight a weak (but still unbeatable) version of the end boss at the beginning of the game, that deals regular level 1 damage in the first 2 rounds and then KO's the player in the third. (Make sure this battle is flagged "Can Lose") The PC wakes up somewhere, all beaten up, maybe with amnesia or a psychic power after a blow to his head. This way the player gets instant action, gets sucked into the story straight away, and have a real WTF moment if they lose a battle 30 seconds into the game. Of course, after that first loss, you should start with easy to beat troops. And this kind of opening works with any kind of end-boss: An alien, a school bully, a mafia boss, satan himself.
Spoiler:
Idea 3: Don't attack
PC starts in battle with a wounded opponent, a princess maybe, or a child, maybe an elderly lady, someone who you should help if they are in pain. The idea is that you're supposed to instinctively heal her and any player who actually reads the dialogue will. However, if a player skips dialogue, they will most likely think: This is a battle, I should attack. When that happens, let the target die, and the player be chased out of the starting area. They are threatened to be attacked on sight if they ever return.
If they are not going to read the dialogue anyway, then they don't need their business, missing out of minor quests and their rewards and some storyline, and most importantly: The tutorial.
All are scripted opening battles, but I think they all catch the players attentions. I have so many ideas but I can't make all the games!
And the wordt is: I had a few more idea's while writing the first one, but while I was done writing the third one, I couldn't remember what those were.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
Personally, I prefer not to be started "in media res".  Mostly because almost everyone botches it, including high paid Hollywood types and AAA game makers.
The other reason I don't like it is because...
I need a reason to be doing whatever I'm doing in the game.  I need set up.
Throwing me immediately into battle usually tells me "dev has no idea what they're doing" or "dev is really bad at storytelling".
How many books and/or movies start in the middle of an action sequence?  Not many.  Of those that do, how many are GOOD movies/books, and aren't just slop?
Without proper set up and context, I find myself highly disinterested in whatever it is you're doing with your game.  Who am I?  Why am I fighting?  Does this even matter?  How does it matter?  Is it just "video game trope tutorial"?  If so... just... ew.
It doesn't have to be long.  It just has to set up the world, the characters I'm immediately going to be spending time with, and my character's motivations, which HOPEFULLY align with the PLAYER MOTIVATIONS.
Always better when I, the player, want to solve the mystery as much as the characters do.  Always better when I, the player, want to defeat the bad guys as much as the characters do.
It's less fun when I'm bored and could care less about the characters and their personal crusades against... whatever.
It isn't enough to "just get me to playing the game as quick as possible".  I get that it's "a game" and "it's meant to be interactive" and Extra Credits (incorrectly) states you should "give the player agency as soon as you can", but...  The specifics of those things matter more than the generalized notion of them.
After all, most people aren't psychopaths and are willing to merc any and everything just because a game labels them as "bad guys".
That's why I quit playing Final Fantasy 12.  And 7.  "Oh, you mean, I'm playing the bad guys?  Eh, no thanks".  FF12 does NOT do a good job of setting up why we'd rebel against the Empire (who has done nothing wrong according to the first 30 hours of the game, except just conquer your nation... they are even treating most people very well, according to the story).  FF7 does NOT do a good job of telling me why it's "good to be an Eco Terrorist".  Or a mercenary who doesn't care about people.
Without proper context, I check out.
Or, you know... if you aren't good at storytelling... just design Diablo or Borderlands 3.  Constant combat, story doesn't matter, it's something you mash "skip" for.  Or... Path of Exile.  Whatever.
But, if you're aiming to tell a story...
Yeah, do it right, please.

posts.author: ZimXero
posts.body:
I don't care as long as the game is good and the cutscenes are under 5 minutes.  Every gamer has been stuck in
cut scenes
that made them late or that they never got finish.  If I can't save within 5 minutes of the start, I usually shelve the game forever.
If you think that is harsh, put everything away and watch a clock for 5 minutes. After you do this you can tell me it is unreasonable.

posts.body:
JohnDoeGames said:

Click to expand...
To be fair...
The only Final Fantasy I played that "starts with battle" that I enjoyed was...
Final Fantasy Mystic Quest.  Which everyone else has usually declared a terrible game
I also don't really enjoy the Kingdom Hearts games.  Too much "mystery box" nonsense going on, and insane incoherencies, all for... what doesn't amount to a story I find very interesting (meaning its impenetrable nature makes it feel "not worth it" to me, when answers finally do come).
And no, I didn't really like "straight into combat" in Kingdom Hearts either.
For me, doing that is usually a good indicator of whether I will find a game to be "fun" or not.
If you gotta jangle keys at me in the first 2 minutes...  I do not anticipate I'll be playing anything interesting or remarkable.  If it does end up "being good", it usually ends up being "niche", too.
JohnDoeGames said:
Battle can be designed as a tutorial.
Click to expand...
It can, but it's rare that this is done well, too...  It's almost always very hand-holdy and requires you basically not learn anything, but instead follow directions specifically to progress.  Or, what is taught is very "not optimal" for combat and gameplay... and instead is some weird brain child system of a dev who isn't a fan of "combat that makes stuff dead" and is instead a fan of "intricate mechanics that make combat take forever".
But, that's a personal preference of mine.
Unless your tutorial is "how to make stuff dead in 1 turn", I don't need it.  Teach me "how to win on turn one" if you need a combat tutorial.
Otherwise, I feel like you're just wasting my time.

posts.author: ClaritasRPG
posts.body:
Avoid long cutscenes etc, throw the player in the game right away. The intro/prologue etc can be made into something that you can play (bonus for also being a tutorial and teaching basic stuff about the game).
If you add long cutscenes, dialogs etc before the actual game starts, you're asking for the player to close and delete the game, unless they know beforehand that it is a good game.

posts.author: Banana_Duck
posts.body: Add an option to skip the introductory cutscene. This can be either a button press or a choice before the cutscene.

posts.author: freakytapir
posts.body:
As you said yourself, Persona 5 does this well, and another good example I found is Expedition 33.
The game cold opens with two character, no cutscene, no background and just takes it from there with good dialogue doing the heavy lifting, combat tutorials breaking up the talking, even an optional miniboss.
And by the time the actual opening cutscenes start to play, I'm already deeply invested in everyone there.
